Why? Because our upbringing, education, religious training, socialization, and the ongoing mind-fuck of news media and authoritative, expert opinion have so monumentally alienated us from ourselves, we don't so much as recognize our true selves when we meet us -- let alone relate to ourselves, understand ourselves, or appreciate ourselves. Why does that thought make us so uncomfortable?

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
This is just one example. People do this shit all the time.

Atheism isn't wrong in asserting there are no gods. 

Atheism is irrational in adopting an identifier that is meaningless without the very idea they're trying to debunk.

Atheists are also greatly misled, because they mistakenly think that attacking a rationalization will affect the motivations and intentions that led to its formation.

“God” isn't something that "believers" believe -- it's a rationalization used to explain and justify what they want to do and are bound to do, "God" or not. 

"God" is an excuse, created by "believers" precisely because they otherwise would have no real clue what to believe -- but believe they must -- so they make up stories and believe those.

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
Some offendedness is legit. Offended ego is not.

I have no obligation to cater to your ego. I have no responsibility for the offense that the truth I tell you might cause your ego.

If the first thing that registers for you is offense that overshadows your honest desire to know what's really going on (aka, truth,) I'm talking about you below.

No one owes your ego shitall.

The biggest egotists of all are people who take up the offense of other egotists, casting them as victims.

Victimhood is egotism. Being victimized is one thing. That's an incident, not a state we capitulate into. Victimhood is a condition of mind in which we lose all track of ourselves, our agency, our power, and our honesty.

Genuine offense creates outrage, not complaint. It has nothing to do with the "injustice" a violator did to us. That's history. Victimhood is transient, short-lived, quickly driving us to do all we can to make sure no one again violates anyone like we were violated. It triggers power and action, not entrapment and pleading that scream for advocacy. The outraged don't need or wait for advocates to stand and speak for them, because you don't bring talkers to an overthrow.

comment.name: Millard J Melnyk
comment.body:
Try it out. Whenever you ask yourself, “Is this a cult?” or whenever you muse, “This seems cultish,” then look to see if the proponents trying to achieve dominance do it by overriding personal experience and judgment with narrative. 

Actually, the fact alone that they’re seeking dominance is a dead giveaway.

If that’s what they’re doing—overriding an individual’s experience and judgment with some “authoritative” narrative—then it’s a cult.

It doesn’t matter how big the group is. Most cults have only 2 members: the cult leader and the cult follower, often called “relationships”. But they’re not.
